node.label: Niall Ferguson
node.date_label: The Pity of War (1998) · Empire: How Britain Made the Modern World (2003) · The Shock of the Global: four-editor collection (2010)
node.description: A historian of war, finance and empire whose work makes counterfactual comparison explicit. In his 2007 conversation with Huw Spanner he argues that historians should state plausible alternatives rather than narrate outcomes as inevitable. He uses that approach to defend a disputed interpretation of Britain’s intervention in 1914 and to appraise imperial outcomes. These judgments remain Ferguson’s claims, including their chosen comparisons and values; the entry does not adopt them as settled verdicts on war or empire. His co-editorship of The Shock of the Global is separately credited.

proposed_edges.relationship: Uses an explicit counterfactual about British nonintervention in 1914 to contest an inevitable-war narrative.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2007 interview answers on alternative futures and The Pity of War. His judgment that a German victory would have been tolerable remains disputed testimony, not this graph’s endorsed conclusion or a current strategic recommendation.

proposed_edges.relationship: Argues that causal explanations should state plausible alternative outcomes and preserve contemporaries’ uncertainty.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own answers to the causation, scientific-method and counterfactual questions. A methodological proposal about explanation, not proof that counterfactuals can be experimentally tested or that every imagined alternative is plausible.
